detail.scope: Commercial-sector electricity sales and average price by state, as reported to EIA. Data centers are billed mostly in the commercial class, so this is a proxy for their load, not a measurement of it.

sources.name: ERCOT
sources.scope: Large generators with a full interconnection study requested, from the monthly Generator Interconnection Status report for Texas. Includes projects from study through commissioning.

sources.name: NYISO
sources.scope: Projects in the New York interconnection queue as NYISO publishes them.

sources.name: MISO
sources.scope: Projects in the Midcontinent generator interconnection queue, all statuses as MISO publishes them.

sources.name: Southwest Power Pool
sources.scope: Generator interconnection requests across the south-central US, all statuses as SPP publishes them, withdrawn requests counted separately.

sources.name: CAISO
sources.scope: Active generator interconnection requests on the California ISO grid, from the public queue report. Completed and withdrawn projects are counted separately.

analysis.body:
The five grid operators whose public interconnection queues are captured here — ERCOT, NYISO, MISO, Southwest Power Pool, and CAISO — together show more than 1.3 million megawatts of generation and storage projects waiting at various stages to connect to the grid as of September 3, 2026. These are planned projects seeking study slots and grid access, not measurements of actual electricity demand, and the operators differ in which project statuses they include, so the queues cannot be added together into a single national total. What the figures do reveal is the direction developers are betting: across ERCOT, MISO, SPP, and CAISO combined, storage requests alone account for more than 328,000 MW of queue capacity, while gas-fired generation across all five operators totals roughly 184,000 MW, a pairing that closely mirrors the kind of around-the-clock, high-density load that large data center campuses require.

Texas's ERCOT queue is the largest single queue in the dataset at roughly 438,000 MW across 1,778 requests, with gas at about 78,000 MW and storage at about 160,000 MW — the largest storage figure of any operator shown. That storage-plus-gas combination in a single-state grid is a notable signal, because data center operators seeking firm, dispatchable power behind the meter or at the campus level have increasingly paired battery systems with gas generation to guarantee uptime. California's CAISO queue, though far smaller at about 71,700 MW across only 265 active requests, shows storage at roughly 46,900 MW, which is 65 percent of its entire active queue by capacity, suggesting that whatever load growth is anticipated on the California grid is expected to be firmed primarily with batteries rather than new gas.

The commercial electricity sales figures reported to EIA for June 2026 offer a rough proxy for where large commercial loads — data centers are billed predominantly in the commercial class — are already drawing power: Texas leads all states shown at about 15,754 gigawatt-hours, followed by California at roughly 10,025 GWh and Virginia at about 7,771 GWh, with average commercial prices ranging from $8.66 per megawatt-hour in Texas to $27.33 in California, a spread that helps explain why interconnection queue volumes skew toward lower-cost states. These sales figures are a proxy, not a direct measurement of data center consumption, and the EIA's scope note makes clear they cover the full commercial sector. Readers tracking AI infrastructure build-out should watch whether ERCOT's gas queue requests — already at 78,000 MW — continue rising in the September and October monthly Generator Interconnection Status reports, as sustained growth there would be the clearest available public signal that large load commitments in Texas are hardening into contracted capacity.
